a:r.a:t: Dietary Fatty Acids Are Absorbed in the Vertebrate Small Intestine

p:cNvPr.descr: An image depicting the processing of dietary lipids in vertebrates. On the top left is a silhouette of a human being with an inset of digestion from the throat down to the gallbladder. Two boxes below that outline the steps of digestion. They are: (1) bile salts emulsify dietary fats in the small intestine, forming mixed micelles; (2) intestinal lipases degrade triacylglycerols; (3) fatty acids and other breakdown products are taken up by the intestinal mucosa and converted into triacylglycerols; (4) triacylglycerols are incorporated, with cholesterol and apolipoproteins, into chylomicrons; (5) Chylomicrons move through the lymphatic system and bloodstream to tissues; (6) lipoprotein lipase, activated by apoC-II in the capillary, converts triacylglycerols to fatty acids and glycerol; (7) fatty acids enter cells, and (8) fatty acids are oxidized as fuel or reesterified for storage. There are insets of the inside of the small intestine, showing ApoC-II and intestinal mucosa. Arrows run from the human inset's stomach through the intestine, and pointing to a chylomicron image and up to a capillary, illustrating the inside with lipoprotein lipase. A line goes through the capillary and points to the chylomicron inside the capillary, which points to an image of storage, CO2, and ATP in an orange oval.
